title: Delhi High Court Orders Takedown of Varun Dhawan AI Deepfakes. The Ruling Names Every Technology That Can Steal a Face.
excerpt: Justice Jyoti Singh's order explicitly targets generative AI, face-morphing, and chatbots — making it one of India's most specific personality rights rulings in the deepfake era.
body:
A Delhi courtroom just drew the clearest line India has between an actor's face and the algorithm that can steal it.

On May 29, Justice Jyoti Singh of the Delhi High Court granted interim relief to Varun Dhawan in a sweeping personality rights case, ordering the takedown of AI-generated deepfakes, unauthorized merchandise, and fake booking listings that had been exploiting the actor's name and image without consent. The ruling is the latest in a growing wave of Indian celebrities seeking legal protection against the digital misuse of their identities — and for the millions of Indian-origin professionals working in tech, the implications hit close to home.

## What the Court Found

The petition named a range of defendants: booking platforms like Hire4Event and Artist Booking Company, which were offering fake appearances by Dhawan; e-commerce sellers on Amazon, Redbubble, and Desertcart peddling unauthorized posters, phone cases, and mugs; and, most alarmingly, websites generating AI-manipulated images and videos depicting the actor in pornographic scenarios.

Justice Singh didn't mince words. "Plaintiff is entitled to protection against dissemination of pornographic content as well as AI-generated images portraying him in an inappropriate scenario," the order stated. "Such distasteful content is harming and damaging the reputation of the plaintiff and may mislead the public into believing what is depicted may be true."

The court restrained all defendants from using Dhawan's name, image, voice, likeness, signature, or any identifiable attribute of his persona — whether through AI, generative AI, machine learning, deepfakes, face-morphing tools, or chatbots — without authorization. Online platforms must remove flagged content within 36 hours of being notified.

## The Bigger Pattern

Dhawan is not the first Bollywood star to seek this protection. Amitabh Bachchan, Anil Kapoor, and most recently Naga Chaitanya have all obtained similar orders from Indian courts. But the Dhawan ruling is notable for how specifically it addresses the AI dimension — naming generative AI, face-morphing, and chatbot technologies by name.

The timing matters. India's Information Technology Act and the 2026 Intermediary Guidelines address synthetically generated content, including deepfakes, but as legal analysts have pointed out, the framework remains reactive. There is no standalone law that defines personality rights, which means each celebrity must fight their own courtroom battle.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, many of whom work in the technology sector that builds these AI tools, the tension is personal. The same generative AI systems being developed in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Silicon Valley can produce convincing deepfakes of anyone — not just Bollywood stars.

Indian courts are, case by case, building a body of precedent that may eventually form the basis of comprehensive personality rights legislation. The Dhawan ruling's explicit naming of AI technologies suggests the judiciary is aware of how fast the threat is evolving.

For NRI families raising children in a world where deepfakes are increasingly trivial to create, the stakes are not abstract. When a Delhi court says that a person's face, voice, and likeness belong to them and not to any algorithm, that principle does not stop at India's borders.

## What Happens Next

All accused individuals and entities have been restrained from the unauthorized use of Dhawan's persona until the next hearing. The formal trial proceedings continue. Senior Advocate Sandeep Sethi, along with a team of IP lawyers, represents Dhawan.

The case will be watched closely — not just in Bollywood, but in the broader conversation about how democracies regulate AI in an era when anyone's identity can be replicated in seconds.
author: Diaspora Desk
